1. Purpose & Scope

The AI-Powered Travel Assistant Planner is a conversational chatbot that collects trip preferences through natural-language extraction — not a fixed questionnaire — and generates a day-by-day itinerary, activity recommendations, transportation guidance, a budget estimate, and a packing checklist. It includes a pre-generation confirmation step and a post-generation review/edit loop that regenerates only the affected section(s).

This document describes the system as implemented in travel_assistant/, covering architecture, the LangGraph conversation flow, the shared state schema, interaction sequences, UI design, technology choices, deployment options, and known limitations.

In scope (per the project proposal): destination selection, adaptive preference collection, itinerary generation, activity recommendations, transportation suggestions, a budget estimate, and a packing checklist — all conversational.

Out of scope: flight/hotel booking, payment processing, visa guidance, live/real-time pricing, and persisting user data or history across sessions.

Figure 2.1 — Component-level architecture. The UI never talks to the model directly; every call is mediated by the graph.

2.2 Why LangGraph instead of an agent loop

The chatbot has a clear multi-stage scope: collect preferences → confirm → itinerary → activities → transportation → budget → packing → review. LangGraph models this as an explicit StateGraph where code controls what happens next via fixed and conditional edges, and the LLM is only ever asked to extract structured fields from one message or generate text for one section at a time.

This is deliberately more constrained than an LLM-driven agent loop, because the project's chosen model (~1B parameters) is not strong enough to reliably plan multi-step tool use on its own. Routing decisions — is a field missing? did the user confirm or ask to edit? — are made by plain Python reading state, never by asking the LLM what to do next.

2.3 Session isolation

Each browser session gets a random thread_id (uuid4, generated in app.py). LangGraph's checkpointer (InMemorySaver) keys all state by thread_id, so multiple users can chat with the deployed demo concurrently without seeing each other's trips. State does not persist across process restarts — this is intentional per the "no persisting user data across sessions" scope constraint.

Whether an incoming message resumes the conversation or starts one is decided by the graph's own checkpoint — graph.get_state(config).next — not by a flag on the session dict. A flag cannot express it: it stayed True once the graph reached END, so every subsequent message was fed to Command(resume=...) on a finished thread, which re-returns the finished state. Asking for a trip to Rome after finalizing a trip to Japan replayed the Japan plan permanently. A thread with no pending next but an existing checkpoint is treated as complete and a fresh thread_id is issued. Gradio's Clear button has the same shape — it wipes the transcript but not gr.State — and is covered by the same rule.

Model loading is lazy. app.get_graph() is @lru_cache-wrapped, so importing app.py — for a test, a lint pass, or CI — no longer downloads and loads a 1B-parameter checkpoint. The first chat message pays the load cost once and every session shares the instance. CI asserts this with an explicit import step.

3. Conversation Workflow (State Machine)

This is the actual graph compiled by build_graph() in travel_assistant/graph.py — fifteen nodes, connected by both fixed edges and three conditional-edge decision points.

3.1 Full graph diagram

Shown as two linked diagrams — the preference-collection/confirmation phase, and the generation/review phase it hands off to — so each renders at a readable scale. Together they are the single graph compiled by build_graph(); confirm_preferences in the first diagram is the same node as the entry point of the second.

flowchart LR START((START)) --> CIR[collect_initial_request] CIR --> EP[extract_preferences] EP --> VP[validate_preferences] VP -->|missing_fields not empty| RMF[request_missing_fields] RMF --> EP VP -->|missing_fields empty| SS[show_summary] SS --> CP[confirm_preferences] CP -->|edit requested| APE[apply_preference_edit] APE --> VP
Figure 3.1a — Preference collection & confirmation phase (loops until confirmed).
flowchart LR CP[confirm_preferences] -->|confirmed| GI[generate_itinerary] GI --> GA[generate_activities] GA --> GT[generate_transportation] GT --> GB[generate_budget] GB --> GP[generate_packing] GP --> RP[review_plan] RP -->|edit requested| APL[apply_plan_edit] APL --> RA[regenerate_affected] RA --> RP RP -->|confirmed| END((END))
Figure 3.1b — Generation pipeline & post-generation review/edit loop (loops until finalized). Together, Figures 3.1a–b are the complete 15-node graph with 3 conditional-edge decision points: validate_preferences, confirm_preferences, review_plan.

3.2 Preference collection loop

collect_initial_request normally just passes through: app.py seeds last_user_input with the user's very first chat message before the graph starts, so there's real content to extract from immediately. Its interrupt() only fires as a fallback (e.g. an empty first message).

extract_preferences makes one LLM call per pass: it sends last_user_input with a system prompt asking for a JSON object of exactly eight fields (destination, trip_length_days, group_type, interests, budget_level, travel_style, travel_season, must_visit_attractions), then merges only the non-null, not-yet-known fields into state — a field already set from an earlier turn is never overwritten.

validate_preferences is pure Python — no LLM call. It recomputes missing_fields (the subset of the five required fields still absent) and collected_fields (a display-only snapshot of every known field) from scratch every pass, so these derived fields can never drift from the underlying typed state. A conditional edge (route_after_validation) reads missing_fields: non-empty → request_missing_fields; empty → show_summary.

request_missing_fields interrupts, naming every already-known field and every still-missing required field, and waits for one reply — which can fill in one field or all remaining fields at once. Graceful degradation: each extraction pass that finds zero new required fields increments extraction_attempts; finding at least one resets it to zero. At 3 unproductive attempts, the node switches to asking about exactly one named field (kind: "single_field_fallback") instead of the full missing list — guarding against an unbounded loop.

3.3 Confirmation gate

show_summary is a pass-through that only updates conversation_stage. confirm_preferences does the actual interrupt, showing the full collected_fields snapshot (kind: "summary_confirmation") and waiting for a confirmation or an edit request.

_is_confirmation() checks the reply against a fixed set of confirmation words/phrases (matched as whole words, e.g. "ok" doesn't false-positive inside "looking"), plus a regex pattern for common affirmative sentence shapes (e.g. "all look right," "everything sounds good") that aren't literally in the word list. If confirmed, confirmation_status → "confirmed" and the conditional edge proceeds to generate_itinerary. Otherwise the reply is treated as an edit request, routed to apply_preference_edit (re-extracts with overwrite=True), and loops back to validate_preferences.

3.4 Generation pipeline

Once preferences are confirmed, five nodes run automatically in sequence, each making exactly one LLM call:

NodeReadsProduces
generate_itinerarydestination, trip length, group, interests, budget, optional contextday-by-day itinerary
generate_activitiesdestination, interests, group, optional context5–8 bulleted attraction/activity picks
generate_transportationdestination, trip length, group, budgetgetting-around guidance
generate_budgettrip length, group, budget levela deterministic rate-table dollar estimate, narrated by the LLM
generate_packingdestination, trip length, group, interests, optional contextbulleted packing checklist

"Optional context" means any of travel_style, travel_season, or must_visit_attractions the user happened to mention — folded into prompts when present, never required.

Deterministic budget math. The dollar figure comes from a fixed rate table (_DAILY_RATE_BY_BUDGET × _GROUP_MULTIPLIER × days) in plain Python; the LLM only writes a short narrative around that number. This keeps the one output users are most likely to sanity-check independent of the small model's arithmetic ability.

Each generation node's core logic lives in a plain _*_update(llm, state) -> dict function (e.g. _itinerary_update), separate from the _make_*_node(llm) closure that wraps it for the graph. This split exists so regenerate_affected (§3.5) can call the same update logic directly on demand, without re-running the whole five-node chain.

3.5 Post-generation review/edit loop

After generate_packing, review_plan interrupts asking "Would you like any changes, or shall I finalize this plan?" (kind: "plan_review"). A confirming reply ends the graph via route_after_review. Any other reply routes to apply_plan_edit.

apply_plan_edit re-runs extraction with overwrite=True, using an edit-specific prompt (_EDIT_EXTRACTION_SYSTEM_PROMPT) that's given the currently known field values as context and instructed to return each changed field's full updated value — merging old and new information rather than replacing it (e.g. "food, museums" + "add outdoor activities" → "food, museums, outdoor activities").

It then diffs the updated fields against the prior state to find which fields actually changed, and maps each changed field to the generation node(s) it affects via _FIELD_TO_REGEN_NODES:

Changed fieldRegenerates
destinationitinerary, activities, transportation, packing
trip_length_daysitinerary, budget, packing
group_typeitinerary, transportation, budget
interestsactivities, packing
budget_levelbudget only
travel_styleitinerary, activities
travel_seasonpacking
must_visit_attractionsitinerary, activities

The resulting node list (regeneration_targets) is deduplicated and reordered to match the canonical generation order. regenerate_affected then calls only those nodes' _*_update functions directly — not the full graph chain — threading each result into the next call's view of state so a request affecting multiple sections sees updates from earlier ones in the same pass. The loop returns to review_plan, allowing several rounds of edits before finalizing.

4. State Schema

travel_assistant/state.py defines the single TravelState shared across every node: 

class TravelState(TypedDict, total=False):
    # Raw conversational input
    last_user_input: Optional[str]

    # Collected from the traveler — required
    destination: Optional[str]
    trip_length_days: Optional[int]
    group_type: Optional[str]
    interests: Optional[str]
    budget_level: Optional[str]

    # Collected from the traveler — optional
    travel_style: Optional[str]
    travel_season: Optional[str]
    must_visit_attractions: Optional[str]

    # Gap-analysis / conversation bookkeeping
    collected_fields: Dict[str, str]
    missing_fields: List[str]
    conversation_stage: ConversationStage
    confirmation_status: Optional[ConfirmationStatus]
    extraction_attempts: int
    regeneration_targets: Optional[List[str]]

    # Produced by the generation nodes
    itinerary: Optional[str]
    activities: Optional[str]
    transportation: Optional[str]
    budget_estimate: Optional[str]
    packing_list: Optional[str]

Field groups

GroupFieldsNotes
Required preferencesdestination, trip_length_days, group_type, interests, budget_levelDrive the gap analysis in validate_preferences; block progress until all 5 are known.
Optional preferencestravel_style, travel_season, must_visit_attractionsNever block progress — folded into prompts if present.
Stated total (not a preference)budget_total_usdAn explicit figure the traveler named ("we have around $4,000"), kept as an int. Never requested, so it stays out of missing_fields; used verbatim by _estimate_budget, and the budget_level tier is back-derived from it. Iterated via DISPLAYED_FIELDS so it is echoed back and diffed on an edit.
Bookkeeping (derived)collected_fields, missing_fieldsRecomputed from scratch on every validate_preferences pass, never mutated incrementally — cannot drift from the typed fields above.
Bookkeeping (stateful)conversation_stage, confirmation_status, extraction_attemptsTrack where the conversation is and bound the extract/re-ask loop.
Bookkeeping (transient)regeneration_targetsPopulated by apply_plan_edit, consumed and cleared by regenerate_affected.
Generated outputsitinerary, activities, transportation, budget_estimate, packing_listWritten once by the generation pipeline; selectively overwritten by regenerate_affected.

ConversationStage values

"collecting" → "extracting" → "awaiting_missing_fields" (loop) → "ready" → "awaiting_confirmation" → "reviewing" → "complete". Set by whichever node last ran; purely descriptive, not read by any routing logic.

ConfirmationStatus is "pending" or "confirmed", used at both the pre-generation confirmation gate and the post-generation review gate.

Closed vocabularies

group_type and budget_level are Literal types (GroupType, GROUP_TYPES; BudgetLevel, BUDGET_LEVELS) rather than free str, because both index into lookup tables — _GROUP_MULTIPLIER and _DAILY_RATE_BY_BUDGET. _normalize_group_type / _normalize_budget_level map free text onto them during extraction; anything unmappable becomes None, returning the field to missing_fields so it is re-asked.

Why this is typed rather than validated later. budget_level was previously free text reaching _DAILY_RATE_BY_BUDGET.get(key, 175). "mid-range", "$4000" and "zzz" therefore all costed out at the moderate rate and produced an identical, confident, wrong figure with nothing in the output to signal it. _estimate_budget now raises ValueError on an unrecognized value: every input is required and normalized by the time generation runs, so an unexpected one is a pipeline bug, not user error, and must not be papered over with a plausible number.

Note the synonym table checks luxury and moderate before budget: "budget" is also the ordinary noun for the field, so "a moderate budget" must not resolve to the cheap tier. When scanning the user's raw message as a fallback, the bare noun is excluded entirely (allow_bare_noun=False) — in "we have around $4,000 budget" it is unambiguously the noun.

5. Interaction Sequences

Two representative sequences: the common case where a single message supplies every required field, and the case where a follow-up round plus a post-generation edit is needed. Both converge on the same confirmation → generation → review path.

5.1 Single-message happy path

sequenceDiagram actor U as User participant UI as Gradio ChatInterface participant G as LangGraph (graph.invoke) participant EP as extract_preferences participant VP as validate_preferences participant CKPT as Checkpointer U->>UI: "7-day family trip to Japan, food + theme parks, moderate budget" UI->>G: invoke({"last_user_input": message}) G->>CKPT: load state (empty for new thread) G->>EP: extract_preferences EP->>G: destination=Japan, days=7, group=family, interests=..., budget=moderate G->>VP: validate_preferences -> missing_fields = [] VP->>G: conditional edge -> show_summary -> confirm_preferences G-->>UI: __interrupt__, kind="summary_confirmation" UI-->>U: "Here's what I have for your trip: ..." U->>UI: "yes, that's correct" UI->>G: invoke(Command(resume=message)) G->>G: confirmed -> generate_itinerary ... generate_packing -> review_plan G-->>UI: __interrupt__, kind="plan_review" UI-->>U: full plan + "Would you like any changes, or shall I finalize?" U->>UI: "looks great, finalize" UI->>G: invoke(Command(resume=message)) G->>CKPT: save final state G-->>UI: full state (no __interrupt__) UI-->>U: format_summary(state) — final trip plan
Figure 5.1 — Happy path: three round-trips total (state, confirm, plan-review) when every field is stated up front.

5.2 Multi-turn path with a post-generation edit

sequenceDiagram actor U as User participant UI as Gradio ChatInterface participant G as LangGraph (graph.invoke) U->>UI: "Family trip to Japan." UI->>G: invoke({"last_user_input": message}) G-->>UI: __interrupt__, kind="missing_fields", missing=[days, interests, budget] UI-->>U: "So far I have destination and group type. Trip length, interests, budget?" U->>UI: "5 days, moderate budget, food and nature" UI->>G: invoke(Command(resume=message)) G-->>UI: __interrupt__, kind="summary_confirmation" — all fields known UI-->>U: "Here's what I have for your trip: ..." U->>UI: "yes" UI->>G: invoke(Command(resume=message)) G-->>UI: __interrupt__, kind="plan_review" (full plan shown) U->>UI: "increase my budget to luxury" UI->>G: invoke(Command(resume=message)) G->>G: apply_plan_edit detects budget_level changed -> regenerate_affected runs only generate_budget G-->>UI: __interrupt__, kind="plan_review" (only budget section changed) U->>UI: "no more changes, finalize" UI->>G: invoke(Command(resume=message)) G-->>UI: full state (no __interrupt__) UI-->>U: format_summary(state) — final trip plan, luxury budget
Figure 5.2 — A missing-fields round-trip plus a selective post-generation regeneration (only the budget section is rewritten).

Implementation detail (travel_assistant/app.py): respond() checks for the "__interrupt__" key in the dict returned by graph.invoke(). If present, _render_interrupt() dispatches on the payload's "kind" key (initial_prompt, missing_fields, single_field_fallback, summary_confirmation, or plan_review) to render the right prompt. If absent, the graph ran to completion and format_summary() renders all five generated sections into one message.

6. Extraction Robustness (Small-Model Hardening)

Because the model is only ~1B parameters, graph.py contains a substantial layer of code-level backstops around the raw LLM extraction call. These are not incidental — they're the difference between a demo that works reliably and one that silently drifts.

6.1 Truncated JSON repair — _extract_json

A small model generating a long field list not infrequently stops before emitting the closing }. Rather than requiring a fully balanced object (which would discard every field in a response, not just the one being generated when it cut off), _extract_json tracks bracket/string depth character-by-character and repairs a still-open object — closing an unterminated string, dropping a dangling trailing comma, closing every open bracket — before parsing.

6.2 Grounding check — _is_grounded

A small model does not reliably follow a "don't guess" instruction. For fields prone to plausible-sounding invention (group_type, budget_level, travel_style, travel_season), _is_grounded requires that at least one meaningful word from the extracted value actually appears in what the user typed — otherwise the value is discarded rather than trusted. destination is deliberately exempt (_UNGROUNDED_FIELDS): destinations are often given as nicknames with no word overlap with the formal name (e.g. "the Big Apple" → "New York"), so grounding would reject too many correct extractions there.

6.3 Deterministic extraction decoding

Extraction calls request greedy decoding (pipeline_kwargs={"do_sample": False}) rather than the model's normal sampling temperature — sampling could otherwise make the model non-deterministically miss an explicitly stated field on some turns and not others. Generation calls (itinerary, activities, etc.) keep the configured temperature for varied, natural text.

6.4 Numeric and categorical fallbacks

HelperHandles
_coerce_trip_length / _find_duration_daysRecognizes spelled-out numbers ("seven-day") when the model's JSON value is null. The raw-text scan requires the number to sit adjacent to a duration noun (day/night/week, allowing up to two intervening adjectives — "5 high-end days"), and converts weeks. A bare digit scan read "Group of 4 going to Tokyo" as a 4-day trip; requiring the unit also picks up "a week" and "two weeks", which no digit scan can find.
_infer_group_type / _normalize_group_typeA fixed keyword table (wife/husband/son/daughter/friends/etc.) infers group_type directly from raw text — "my wife and son" → "family" — since the small model doesn't reliably categorize, and the grounding check would reject it even if it did (the word "family" never appears literally). The same table normalizes whatever the model did return ("a family of four" → family), because the value indexes into _GROUP_MULTIPLIER.
_normalize_budget_levelMaps free text onto BUDGET_LEVELS using word-boundary matching, and a stricter vocabulary for the raw message than for the model's own answer. Substring matching was a live defect found in review — "mid" fired inside pyramids and "low" inside flower, so a message that never mentioned money silently acquired a tier, skipped the question, and was costed at the invented rate. Also applied to the raw message as a fallback: _is_grounded runs before normalization and tokenizes the model's answer, so for "a moderate budget" answered "mid-range" the tokens {mid, range} appear nowhere in the message and the field is nulled — dropping a preference the user stated outright. group_type survives this via its raw-text backstop; budget_level needed the same one.
_find_dollar_amountCaptures an explicit total as an int into budget_total_usd — its own field, not budget_level. Storing "$4,000" as the tier was how a stated budget came to be silently costed at the default moderate rate. Rejects per-unit rates ("$200 a night", "$800 each") and parses magnitude suffixes ("$4.5k" → 4500): since a stated total is returned verbatim by _estimate_budget, reading a nightly rate as the total would cap a seven-day family trip at $200.
_looks_like_specific_placeRejects a must_visit_attractions value that isn't Title Case — real place names extract reliably in Title Case; generic themes misfiled into this field ("food", "hiking") don't — and recovers the value into interests instead.

6.7 Budget narration verification

The generation prompt instructs the model not to invent dollar figures, and a ~1B model ignores that instruction often enough to matter. Observed against a stated $5,000 budget: "we're estimating a total of approximately $1,200"; and separately "$1,800 - $2,200 per night for 3 nights … would be approximately $540 - $720 total" — self-contradictory arithmetic presented with full confidence.

_conflicting_amounts scans the returned prose for dollar figures that disagree with the authoritative total. If any are found the entire narration is discarded in favour of _budget_fallback_text, a deterministic sentence, and a WARNING is logged. The budget is the one output users are most likely to check, so the same principle that keeps the figure out of the model's hands is extended to the prose around it — a code-level backstop for a failure a prompt cannot prevent, exactly as with _is_grounded. The WARNING rate is also the metric for whether a larger model still needs the backstop.

6.5 Edit-time group_type override

During an edit (overwrite=True), the model sometimes just echoes back the previous group_type unchanged instead of recognizing the edit text as a change (e.g. "will only go byself" left a prior group_type of "family" untouched). _merge_extracted re-runs _infer_group_type on the edit text even when overwrite=True, and a keyword match there overrides the model's possibly-stale returned value.

6.6 Extraction attempt bounding

extraction_attempts increments on any pass that finds zero new required fields and resets to zero on any pass that finds at least one. At _MAX_EXTRACTION_ATTEMPTS = 3, request_missing_fields switches from asking for everything still missing to asking about exactly one named field — the graceful-degradation path described in §3.2.

7. UI Design

A single Gradio ChatInterface (travel_assistant/app.py) — no separate screens or forms. The chat window opens with a pre-seeded assistant greeting introducing what the assistant can do, and invites a free-form trip description rather than a first question.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ AI-Powered Travel Assistant Planner │ │ Tell me about the trip you would like to plan. │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Assistant: Hi! I'm your AI travel planning assistant. │ │ Tell me about the trip you'd like to take — │ │ destination, days, who's going, interests, │ │ and budget — and I'll take care of the rest. │ │ User: 7-day family trip to Japan, we love food and │ │ theme parks, moderate budget. │ │ Assistant: Here's what I have for your trip: destination │ │ (Japan), trip length (7 days), group type │ │ (family), interests (food and theme parks), │ │ and budget (moderate). Does that all look │ │ right, or would you like to change anything? │ │ User: yes │ │ Assistant: ## Your trip to Japan │ │ **Itinerary** ... │ │ **Activities** ... │ │ **Getting around** ... │ │ **Estimated budget** ... │ │ **Packing checklist** ... │ │ Would you like any changes, or shall I │ │ finalize this plan? │ │ User: finalize │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ [ type a message... ] [ Send ] │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Figure 7.1 — Chat window mockup, happy path.

If the first message is missing required fields, the assistant responds in plain sentences rather than a form-style list:

Great! So far I have your destination (Japan) and group type (family). Could you tell me your trip length, interests, and budget? Feel free to share one or all of those in your next message.

Both messages are produced by _render_interrupt() in app.py (_describe_known/_describe_missing turn field lists into a comma-and-"and" phrase). An earlier revision used a ✅/❓ checklist card for the same information, but that read as a form rather than something a person would say, so it was replaced with conversational prose.

HCI heuristics considered

HeuristicHow it's applied
Visibility of system statusEvery response during collection/confirmation names every known and missing field in prose.
Match between system & real worldOpening prompt invites a natural trip description instead of a form-style question.
Recognition rather than recallConfirmation and review cards show everything already collected.
User control & freedomTwo explicit review points (confirm_preferences, review_plan) let the user correct course without restarting.
Flexibility & efficiency of useA user who states every field at once resolves in one turn; a partial user is asked only for what's missing.
Error prevention over recovery_coerce_trip_length and _extract_json degrade gracefully instead of crashing the turn.
ConsistencyEvery generated section uses the same heading style; the same "known, then missing" phrasing pattern is reused throughout.

_merge_extracted(llm, state, overwrite)graph.pyThe single extraction routine used by both initial collection (overwrite=False) and edits (overwrite=True).
_estimate_budget(state)graph.pyTotal in USD. Returns budget_total_usd verbatim when the traveler stated one; otherwise the deterministic rate-table product. Raises on an unnormalized input rather than defaulting.
_derive_budget_level(state)graph.pyBack-derives the tier from a stated total once trip length and group are known, so naming a figure doesn't also trigger a redundant tier question.
_conflicting_amounts(text, total)graph.pyFinds dollar figures in the model's narration that disagree with the authoritative total; triggers the deterministic fallback sentence.
_find_duration_days(text)graph.pyTrip length read only from an explicit duration phrase — never a stray digit.
format_summary(state)graph.pyRenders the five generated sections into one chat message. Used both by the plan_review card and by the finalized reply.
get_graph()app.py@lru_cached lazy build — keeps import app free of a model load.
respond(message, history, session)app.pyGradio callback. Chooses resume vs. fresh start from graph.get_state(config).next, and converts LLMInvocationError/node failures into user-facing messages.

9. Deployment & Runtime Environments

The system has no server component beyond the Gradio process itself — no database, no external API keys, no persisted storage. Deployment is simply "run the Gradio app somewhere with a Python environment and enough compute to run a 1B-parameter model."

flowchart LR subgraph Colab["Google Colab (free T4 GPU)"] direction TB NB[travel_assistant_colab.ipynb] --> CUDA_APP[python -m travel_assistant.app] CUDA_APP --> CUDA_MODEL["unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-bnb-4bit
(4-bit, bitsandbytes + accelerate)"] end subgraph Local["Local machine"] direction TB LOCAL_APP[python -m travel_assistant.app] --> DEVICE{Detected backend} DEVICE -->|CUDA GPU| CUDA_MODEL2["unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-bnb-4bit"] DEVICE -->|Apple Silicon MPS| MPS_MODEL["unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct
fp16, native PyTorch pipeline"] DEVICE -->|CPU only| CPU_MODEL["unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct
fp32, slow but functional"] end Browser["User's browser"] -->|gradio.live public URL / localhost| CUDA_APP Browser -->|localhost:7860| LOCAL_APP
Figure 9.1 — Deployment topology: same codebase, backend auto-selected by llm.py at process start.

9.1 Backend auto-detection

_pick_device() in llm.py checks torch.cuda.is_available(), then torch.backends.mps.is_available(), falling back to CPU. The model checkpoint choice follows the device:

BackendModelWhy
CUDA (e.g. Colab T4)unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-bnb-4bitThe proposal's pre-quantized checkpoint; bitsandbytes 4-bit quantization requires CUDA kernels. Loaded via HuggingFacePipeline.from_model_id(device_map="auto") so accelerate handles dispatch.
Apple Silicon (MPS)unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (fp16)bitsandbytes has no Metal backend. Loaded via a pipeline built directly (not from_model_id(device=...), which only accepts legacy CUDA integer indices, not device strings like "mps").
CPUunsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (fp32)Same non-quantized weights; functional but slow. Used automatically when no GPU is present.

Any of these defaults can be overridden without a code change by setting TRAVEL_ASSISTANT_MODEL. Resolution order is the explicit model_id argument, then the environment variable, then the per-device default. This exists so a candidate model can be pointed at the eval harness (TRAVEL_ASSISTANT_MODEL=… python -m evals.extraction_eval) and compared on numbers rather than argued about — the 1B default is what the proposal specifies and what the architecture is designed around, so a larger model is an upgrade rather than a prerequisite.

9.2 Environments

Google Colab (recommended for teammates without local GPU)

  1. Enable the free T4 GPU: Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU.
  2. Get the code in — either upload travel_assistant_project.zip and unzip, or clone the repo directly from GitHub (always latest main).
  3. Run all notebook cells top to bottom; the first run downloads the model (a couple of minutes, once per session).
  4. Open the printed public https://xxxxx.gradio.live link.

Local (Apple Silicon / CUDA / CPU)

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m travel_assistant.app

Opens at localhost:7860. Verified end-to-end on Apple M4 Max (64 GB) via the MPS backend, no cloud dependency.

Logic-only (no model download — CI and quick checks)

pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
pytest
ruff check . && ruff format --check .
Keeping the zip snapshot fresh. travel_assistant_project.zip is a point-in-time snapshot for Colab Option A, not a live link to the code. If travel_assistant/ changes, regenerate it before teammates rely on it — command is in the README.

10. Testing & Evaluation Strategy

Two layers, answering two different questions. Tests ask "does the conversation flow behave?" and fake the model out entirely. Evals ask "is the model any good at its job?" and require the real one. Neither substitutes for the other.

10.1 Unit tests — conversation logic

163 tests, no GPU, no download. A fake chat model branches on the system prompt text: extraction calls get a small regex-based fake extractor, generation calls get an echoed prompt snippet.

FileCovers
tests/test_graph.pyGraph control flow, extraction merging, normalization, duration parsing, the budget backstop.
tests/test_app.pySession lifecycle, interrupt rendering, error handling.
tests/test_llm.pyModel-selection resolution (no weights loaded).
tests/test_extraction_eval.pyThe eval scorer itself — a harness that miscounted a hallucination as a hit would report a confident number that means nothing.
pytest
ruff check . && ruff format --check .

The safety-critical assertion is that requesting a change to one part of the finished plan (e.g. "increase my budget") regenerates only the mapped section(s) via _FIELD_TO_REGEN_NODES, leaving the rest of the plan untouched.

CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs ruff + pytest on Python 3.11–3.13 with CPU-only torch, plus an explicit import travel_assistant.app step. That import is a regression guard: the model is built lazily in app.get_graph(), and moving build_chat_model() back to module scope would make CI download a 1B checkpoint and time out.

10.2 Extraction evals — model quality

evals/extraction_cases.json holds ~30 labelled utterances; evals/extraction_eval.py scores _merge_extracted against them per field. A null expectation is a real expectation, so outcomes split four ways:

OutcomeMeaning
hitExpected a value, got a matching one.
missExpected a value, got nothing.
wrongExpected a value, got a different one.
hallucinationExpected nothing, got a value.
Why hallucination is scored separately. A model that invents group_type="solo" for a message that never said who is travelling is far more damaging than one returning null: null triggers a follow-up question, whereas an invented value flows silently into the itinerary, the transport advice and the budget multiplier. Declining to guess is a success, not a failure.

Baseline — 33 cases, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct fp16 on Apple M4 Max:

MetricValue
Field accuracy (hit / expected-a-value)95.2% (99/104)
Hallucination rate (invented / should-be-null)0.0% (0/44)
Fully correct cases28/33
Wrong values0
Mean extraction latency0.90 s

Zero "wrong" is the number to read: when this pipeline produces a value it is correct, and every failure is a miss — it declined rather than guessed. That is §6's hardening doing its job, and it is the desired shape, because a miss becomes a follow-up question while a wrong value becomes a silently bad plan.

The eval paid for itself on its first run, which scored 93.9% with one hallucination: "Group of 4 going to Tokyo" was read as a 4-day trip, because _coerce_trip_length scanned the message for any digit. _find_duration_days now requires the number to sit adjacent to a duration noun, which removed that hallucination and picked up "a week" / "two weeks" as a bonus — 93.9% → 95.2%, 2.3% → 0%, 25 → 28 fully correct.

The checkpoint is selectable via TRAVEL_ASSISTANT_MODEL, so "would a larger model help?" is answered by re-running the eval rather than by argument. The code-level backstops should be kept regardless of model size: they are cheap and deterministic, and a larger model reduces how often they fire without making them unnecessary.

10.3 Manual end-to-end runs

Neither layer replaces driving the real demo. Four user-visible defects were found only by running it — the invisible-plan review, the finalized-plan replay, the dropped stated total, and the budget narration inventing figures. Each now has a regression test.

What is still not covered: factual accuracy of generated itinerary content (the 1B model's claims about specific venues are not verified), and performance under concurrent load.

11. Known Limitations / Out of Scope

Per the proposal: no flight/hotel booking, no payment processing, no visa guidance, no live pricing or availability, not a replacement for a travel agent. Additionally, as currently designed:

  • Extraction quality ceiling. Depends on the local 1B model's ability to follow the JSON-output instruction reliably. extraction_attempts bounds the worst case (falls back to a single named field after 3 unproductive attempts) but doesn't eliminate occasional re-prompts if the model's JSON is malformed.
  • interests vs. must_visit_attractions confusion. The model frequently misfiles a generic theme ("food") into must_visit_attractions instead of interests. _looks_like_specific_place (§6.4) recovers most of these, but the underlying confusion is a model limitation, not something fully eliminated.
  • Confirmation-phrase coverage. _is_confirmation() matches a fixed word/phrase list plus one regex pattern; a phrasing outside both is treated as an edit request instead — which, if it contains no recognizable field change, leaves state unchanged and can look like the assistant ignoring a confirmation.
  • Free-text preference values are unvalidated. group_type and budget_level are now closed vocabularies (§4), but destination, interests, travel_style, travel_season and must_visit_attractions are taken at face value — they feed prompts rather than lookup tables, so there is no vocabulary to check against. A nonsensical destination is passed to the model as written.
  • Generated content is not fact-checked. The budget figure is deterministic and the narration around it is verified (§6.7), but venue names, opening hours and similar claims inside the itinerary and activity sections are whatever the 1B model produced. The eval set measures extraction accuracy, not generation factuality.
  • No mid-collection jump-back. There's no way to jump back into mid-collection editing before the summary is reached short of continuing to answer — but the summary and post-generation review stages both fully support corrections.
  • Model output quality. Weaker factual grounding than a larger model — acceptable for this course project's scope, worth noting in a results report.
  • No session persistence. State lives only in the in-memory checkpointer for the life of the process; restarting the app loses all in-progress conversations (by design — out of scope per the proposal).

12. Design History: Fixed Questionnaire → Adaptive Extraction

The Week 2 implementation used a fixed sequential questionnaire: one field asked at a time, in hard-coded order, regardless of what the user had already volunteered. It worked, but read as a form rather than a conversational assistant.

12.1 The redesign argument

Replace question-by-question delivery with adaptive information extraction: the user describes their trip in free text; one LLM call extracts whatever structured fields it can; a pure-Python gap analysis determines what's still missing; the system asks only for that, accepting any number of fields in a single reply, in any order.

HeuristicFixed questionnaireAdaptive extraction
Visibility of system statusOne question at a time; no overall progress senseEvery turn shows all required fields, known and missing
Match between system & real worldPlain-language but rigid one-field-per-turnMirrors describing a trip to a human agent in one message
User control & freedomCannot answer out of orderAny subset of fields, any order, across 1+ messages
Flexibility & efficiencyA front-loading user gets no benefit — still asked all 5Front-loading skips the clarification loop entirely
Recognition rather than recallMust recall what's already been askedResponse always restates what's already known

Interaction cost drops from a fixed O(5) turns to O(missing fields after the first message) — typically 0–2 follow-up turns for a message that states most fields up front.

12.2 What was, and wasn't, built from the earlier docx proposal

ProposedStatus
Post-generation review/modify with selective regenerationBuilt — as review_plan → apply_plan_edit → regenerate_affected, same idea, different node names.
Input-validation-by-degradation (invalid response → re-ask)Built — via extraction_attempts bounding, not a dedicated validation node.
must_visit_attractions optional fieldBuilt exactly as proposed (with the recovery logic in §6.4 needed in practice).
Pre-generation confirmation gateBuilt — added during implementation, one stage earlier than the docx's own review stage.
user_name / name personalizationNot built — no such field in TravelState.
recommend_destination branchNot built — destination is a required field like any other.
Separate vacation_type fieldDeliberately rejected — duplicate of interests.
Separate "destination known vs. undecided" booleanDeliberately rejected — redundant with missing_fields already expressing destination is None.
